**Micron Technology, Inc.** is an American multinational [semiconductor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semiconductor_industry "Semiconductor industry") company that manufactures [computer memory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer_memory "Computer memory") and [computer data storage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer_data_storage "Computer data storage") products, including [dynamic random-access memory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dynamic_random-access_memory "Dynamic random-access memory") (DRAM), [flash memory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flash_memory "Flash memory"), [High Bandwidth Memory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_Bandwidth_Memory "High Bandwidth Memory") (HBM), and [solid-state drives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solid-state_drive "Solid-state drive") (SSDs). Founded in 1978 in [Boise, Idaho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boise,_Idaho "Boise, Idaho"), Micron is the only major American computer memory manufacturer.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micron_Technology#cite_note-CNBCMicron2023-3) It is one of the "Big Three" computer memory manufacturers, along with the South Korean companies [Samsung Electronics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samsung_Electronics "Samsung Electronics") and [SK Hynix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SK_Hynix "SK Hynix").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micron_Technology#cite_note-4)
Micron marketed its consumer products under the brand **Crucial** , with the sub-brand Ballistix being used to denote products targeting [gaming computers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaming_computer "Gaming computer"), until its disestablishment in 2026. Micron and [Intel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intel "Intel") together created [IM Flash Technologies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IM_Flash_Technologies "IM Flash Technologies"), which produced [NAND flash memory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAND_flash_memory "NAND flash memory"). It owned [Lexar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lexar "Lexar") between 2006 and 2017.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micron_Technology#cite_note-lexar_sale-5)
[Sanjay Mehrotra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanjay_Mehrotra "Sanjay Mehrotra") has served as president and CEO of Micron since 2017.
On May 26, 2026, Micron became the latest U.S. company to reach a US$1 trillion market capitalization, amid surging demand for its [HBM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_Bandwidth_Memory "High Bandwidth Memory") chips.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micron_Technology#cite_note-6)
## History
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Micron_Technology&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]
### 1978–1999
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Micron_Technology&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: 1978–1999")]
Micron was founded in Boise, Idaho, in 1978[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micron_Technology#cite_note-Milestones-7) by Ward Parkinson, Joe Parkinson, Dennis Wilson, and Doug Pitman as a semiconductor design consulting company.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micron_Technology#cite_note-8) Startup funding was provided by local Idaho businessmen Tom Nicholson, Allen Noble, Rudolph Nelson, and Ron Yanke. Later it received funding from Idaho billionaire [J. R. Simplot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._R._Simplot "J. R. Simplot"), whose fortune was made in the [potato](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potato "Potato") business. In 1981, the company moved from consulting to manufacturing with the completion of its first [wafer fabrication](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semiconductor_fabrication_plant "Semiconductor fabrication plant") unit ("Fab 1"), producing 64K DRAM chips.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micron_Technology#cite_note-CNBCMicron2023-3)
In 1984, the company had its [initial public offering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Initial_public_offering "Initial public offering").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micron_Technology#cite_note-9)
Micron sought to enter the market for [RISC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RISC "RISC") processors in 1991 with a product known as FRISC, targeting embedded control and signal processing applications. Running at 80 MHz and described as "a 64-bit processor with fast context-switching time and high floating-point performance", the design supported various features for timely interrupt handling and featured an arithmetic unit capable of handling both integer and floating-point calculations with a claimed throughput of 80 MFLOPS for double-precision arithmetic. Micron aimed to provide a "board-level demonstration supercomputer" in configurations with 256 MB or 1 GB of RAM.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micron_Technology#cite_note-computerdesign19910501_micron-10) Having set up a subsidiary and with the product being designed into graphics cards and accelerators, Micron concluded in 1992 that the effort would not deliver the "best bang for the buck", reassigning engineers to other projects and discontinuing the endeavour.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micron_Technology#cite_note-unigramx19920824_micron-11)
In 1994, founder Joe Parkinson retired as [CEO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chief_executive_officer "Chief executive officer") and [Steve Appleton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Appleton "Steve Appleton") took over as [Chairman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chairman "Chairman"), [President](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_\(corporate_title\) "President \(corporate title\)"), and CEO.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micron_Technology#cite_note-Milestones-7)
A 1996 3-way merger among [ZEOS International](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zeos "Zeos"), Micron Computer, and Micron Custom Manufacturing Services (MCMS) increased the size and scope of the company;[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micron_Technology#cite_note-Milestones-7) this was followed rapidly with the 1997 acquisition of NetFrame Systems, in a bid to enter the mid-range server industry.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micron_Technology#cite_note-12) Between 1998 and 2000, the company was the main sponsor of the [MicronPC Bowl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop-Tarts_Bowl "Pop-Tarts Bowl"), or MicronPC.com Bowl.
### Since 2000
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Micron_Technology&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Since 2000")]
In 2000, [Gurtej Singh Sandhu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gurtej_Sandhu "Gurtej Sandhu") and Trung T. Doan at Micron initiated the development of [atomic layer deposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition "Atomic layer deposition") high-k [films](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thin_film "Thin film") for [DRAM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dynamic_random-access_memory "Dynamic random-access memory") memory devices. This helped drive cost-effective implementation of [semiconductor memory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semiconductor_memory "Semiconductor memory"), starting with [90 nm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/90_nanometer "90 nanometer") [node](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semiconductor_node "Semiconductor node") DRAM.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micron_Technology#cite_note-ieee-1)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micron_Technology#cite_note-13) Pitch [double-patterning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Double_patterning "Double patterning") was also pioneered by Gurtej Singh Sandhu at Micron during the 2000s, leading to the development of [30-nm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/32_nanometer "32 nanometer") class [NAND flash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAND_flash "NAND flash") memory, and it has since been widely adopted by NAND flash and [RAM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RAM "RAM") manufacturers worldwide.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micron_Technology#cite_note-ieee-1)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micron_Technology#cite_note-14)
In 2002, Micron spun off its personal computer business as [MPC Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MPC_Corporation "MPC Corporation") and put it up for sale.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micron_Technology#cite_note-15)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micron_Technology#cite_note-16) The company found the business difficult as the number 12 American computer maker with only 1.3 percent of the market.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micron_Technology#cite_note-17)
Micron and Intel created a joint venture in 2005, based in [IM Flash Technologies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IM_Flash_Technologies "IM Flash Technologies") in [Lehi, Utah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lehi,_Utah "Lehi, Utah").[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micron_Technology#cite_note-18) The two companies formed another joint venture in 2011, [IM Flash Singapore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IM_Flash_Singapore "IM Flash Singapore"), in Singapore.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micron_Technology#cite_note-19) In 2012 Micron became sole owner of this second joint venture.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micron_Technology#cite_note-20) In 2006 Micron acquired [Lexar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lexar "Lexar"), an American manufacturer of digital media products.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micron_Technology#cite_note-lexar_acquire-21)
The company changed leadership again in June 2007 with COO [Mark Durcan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Durcan "Mark Durcan") becoming president.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micron_Technology#cite_note-22) In 2008, Micron converted the Avezzano [chip fab](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chip_fab "Chip fab"), formerly a [Texas Instruments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Instruments "Texas Instruments") DRAM fab, into a production facility for [CMOS image sensors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CMOS_image_sensor "CMOS image sensor") sold by [Aptina Imaging](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aptina "Aptina").[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micron_Technology#cite_note-Lammers-23)
In 2008, Micron spun off Aptina Imaging, which was acquired by [ON Semiconductor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ON_Semiconductor "ON Semiconductor") in 2014. Micron retained a stake in the spinoff.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micron_Technology#cite_note-24) However, the core company suffered setbacks and had to lay off 15 percent of its workforce in October 2008,[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micron_Technology#cite_note-25)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micron_Technology#cite_note-26) during which period the company also announced the purchase of [Qimonda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qimonda "Qimonda")'s 35.6 percent stake in [Inotera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inotera "Inotera") Memories for $400 million.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micron_Technology#cite_note-27) The trend of layoffs and acquisitions continued in 2009 with the termination of an additional 2,000 employees,[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micron_Technology#cite_note-28)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micron_Technology#cite_note-29) and the acquisition of the FLCOS microdisplay company Displaytech.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micron_Technology#cite_note-30) Micron agreed to buy flash-chip maker [Numonyx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numonyx "Numonyx") for $1.27 billion in stock in February 2010.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micron_Technology#cite_note-31)
On February 3, 2012, CEO Appleton died in a plane crash shortly after takeoff from the [Boise Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boise_Airport "Boise Airport"). He was the pilot and sole occupant of the [Lancair IV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lancair_IV "Lancair IV") aircraft.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micron_Technology#cite_note-32)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micron_Technology#cite_note-33)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micron_Technology#cite_note-34) Mark Durcan replaced Appleton as the CEO shortly thereafter,[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micron_Technology#cite_note-35) eliminating his former title of president.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micron_Technology#cite_note-36)
In 2013, the Avezzano chip fab was sold to LFoundry.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micron_Technology#cite_note-Lammers-23) In the 2012 to 2014 period, Micron again went through an acquisition-layoff cycle, becoming the majority shareholder of Inotera Memories, purchasing [Elpida Memory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elpida_Memory "Elpida Memory")[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micron_Technology#cite_note-elpida-37) for $2 billion and the remaining shares in Rexchip, a PC memory chip manufacturing venture between [Powerchip](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Powerchip "Powerchip") and Elpida Memory for $334 million,[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micron_Technology#cite_note-38)[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micron_Technology#cite_note-39) while announcing plans to lay off approximately 3,000 workers.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micron_Technology#cite_note-40)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micron_Technology#cite_note-41) Through the Elpida acquisition, Micron became a major supplier to [Apple Inc.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc. "Apple Inc.") for the [iPhone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IPhone "IPhone") and [iPad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IPad "IPad").[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micron_Technology#cite_note-elpida-37) In December 2016 Micron finished acquiring the remaining 67 percent of [Inotera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inotera "Inotera"), making it a 100 percent subsidiary of Micron.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micron_Technology#cite_note-42)
In April 2017, Micron announced [Sanjay Mehrotra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanjay_Mehrotra "Sanjay Mehrotra") as the new president and CEO to replace [Mark Durcan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Durcan "Mark Durcan").[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micron_Technology#cite_note-43)[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micron_Technology#cite_note-44) In June 2017 Micron announced it was discontinuing the Lexar retail removable media storage business and putting some or all of it up for sale.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micron_Technology#cite_note-45) In August of that year the Lexar brand was acquired by Longsys, a flash memory company based in Shenzhen, China.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micron_Technology#cite_note-lexar_sale-5)
In May 2018, Micron Technology and Intel launched QLC NAND memory to increase storage density.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micron_Technology#cite_note-46) The company ranked 150th on the [Fortune 500](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fortune_500 "Fortune 500") list of largest United States corporations by revenue.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micron_Technology#cite_note-47)
In February 2019, the first [microSD card](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MicroSD_card "MicroSD card") with a storage capacity of 1 [terabyte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terabyte "Terabyte") (TB) was announced by Micron.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micron_Technology#cite_note-48) As of March 2020 3.84TB Micron 5210 Ion is the cheapest large-capacity SSD in the world.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micron_Technology#cite_note-49) In September 2020 the company introduced the world's fastest discrete graphics memory solution. Working with computing technology leader Nvidia, Micron debuted GDDR6X in the [Nvidia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nvidia "Nvidia") GeForce RTX 3090 and GeForce RTX 3080 graphics processing units (GPUs).[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micron_Technology#cite_note-50) In November 2020, the company unveiled a new 176-layer 3D NAND module. It offers improved read and write latency and is slated to be used in the production of a new generation of solid-state drives.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micron_Technology#cite_note-51)
On October 22, 2021, Micron closed the sale of IM Flash's Lehi, Utah fab to [Texas Instruments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Instruments "Texas Instruments") for a sale price of US$900 million.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micron_Technology#cite_note-52) In February 2022, Micron announced that it would discontinue its Ballistix gaming brand.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micron_Technology#cite_note-53) With the passage of the [CHIPS and Science Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CHIPS_and_Science_Act "CHIPS and Science Act"), Micron announced its pledge to invest billions in new manufacturing within the United States.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micron_Technology#cite_note-54) In September 2022, Micron announced it would invest $15 billion in a new facility in [Boise, Idaho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boise,_Idaho "Boise, Idaho").[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micron_Technology#cite_note-55) In October 2022, Micron announced a $100 billion expansion in [Clay, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clay,_New_York "Clay, New York").[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micron_Technology#cite_note-56)[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micron_Technology#cite_note-57)
Micron Technology owed [Netlist, Inc.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netlist,_Inc. "Netlist, Inc.") $445 million in damages for infringing Netlist's patents related to memory-module technology for high-performance computing.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micron_Technology#cite_note-58)[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micron_Technology#cite_note-59) The jury found that Micron's semiconductor-memory products violated two of Netlist's patents willfully, potentially allowing the judge to triple the damages. Netlist had sued Micron in 2022, accusing three of its memory-module lines of patent infringement, which Micron denied, also arguing the patents' invalidity. The U.S. Patent and Trademark Office invalidated one patent in April 2024.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micron_Technology#cite_note-60)
On June 30, 2026, Micron announced they would be investing $250 million in Trump Accounts, which include employee contribution matching and seed funding for eligible children in local communities.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micron_Technology#cite_note-61)
In July 2026, Micron increased its planned United States investment to more than US$250 billion through 2035. The expanded programme included US$3 billion for the domestic semiconductor supply chain, of which US$500 million was allocated to support [GlobalWafers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GlobalWafers "GlobalWafers")' 300 mm silicon-wafer manufacturing facility in [Sherman, Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sherman,_Texas "Sherman, Texas"). Micron and GlobalWafers also agreed to a ten-year wafer-supply arrangement.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micron_Technology#cite_note-62)

In December 2025, Micron announced it will discontinue the Crucial brand and exit the consumer market in February 2026 and focus on enterprise markets including data centers and artificial intelligence.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micron_Technology#cite_note-63)[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micron_Technology#cite_note-64)
On January 27, 2026, Micron Technology committed approximately $24 billion to expand its wafer manufacturing operations in Singapore, adding 700,000 square feet of cleanroom space at an existing NAND manufacturing complex.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micron_Technology#cite_note-65)
As of 2026, Micron is making significant investments in chip-making facilities in the United States, including $200 billion in total commitment. ### Lawsuits
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Micron_Technology&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Lawsuits")]
#### Fujian Jinhua
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Micron_Technology&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Fujian Jinhua")]
On December 5, 2017 Micron sued rivals United Microelectronics Corporation and [Fujian Jinhua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fujian_Jinhua_Integrated_Circuit "Fujian Jinhua Integrated Circuit") Integrated Circuit Co. (JHICC) in the United States District Court for the Northern District of California, alleging infringement on its DRAM patents and intellectual property rights.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micron_Technology#cite_note-67) The U.S. Justice Department in 2018 announced an indictment against Fujian Jinhua, and authorities added the Chinese firm to the Entity List the same year. Fujian Jinhua vehemently denied the claims, saying it had not stolen any technology, and that "Micron regards the development of Fujian Jinhua as a threat and adopts various means to hamper and destroy the development of Fujian Jinhua."[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micron_Technology#cite_note-68)
In May 2023, the [Cyberspace Administration of China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyberspace_Administration_of_China "Cyberspace Administration of China") barred major Chinese information infrastructure firms from purchasing Micron products, citing significant national security risks.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micron_Technology#cite_note-wsj-china-69) The move was seen as retaliation against [US sanctions on China's semiconductor industry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_sanctions_against_China#Sanctions_on_Chinese_semiconductor_industry "United States sanctions against China") and [related export controls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_New_Export_Controls_on_Advanced_Computing_and_Semiconductors_to_China "United States New Export Controls on Advanced Computing and Semiconductors to China").[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micron_Technology#cite_note-70)[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micron_Technology#cite_note-wsj-china-69) In November 2023 Chinese chipmaker [Yangtze Memory Technologies Corp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yangtze_Memory_Technologies "Yangtze Memory Technologies") (YMTC) filed a lawsuit against Micron alleging infringement of eight of its patents.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micron_Technology#cite_note-71)
On February 27, 2024, Judge [Maxine Chesney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maxine_M._Chesney "Maxine M. Chesney") of the [U.S. Federal District Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Federal_District_Court "U.S. Federal District Court") in San Francisco acquitted Fujian Jinhua Integrated Circuit, whom Micron had sued for IP theft, of the charge in a non-jury verdict, believing that there was insufficient evidence to support the charge.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micron_Technology#cite_note-72)[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micron_Technology#cite_note-73)
